feedback: For the spectrum, order by the physical quantity (frequency/wavelength), not just 'rainbow order'.
For red+green spotlights, the answer is yellow; expecting brown conflates subtractive pigment mixing with additive light mixing.
For the red filter, it TRANSMITS red and ABSORBS the rest — it does not dye all the light red.
For the prism, dispersion separates colours already present because each frequency refracts by a different amount; it does not create colour.
Treat 'black' as the idealised limiting case — real pigments and lights give 'very dark', not perfectly black.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the subtractive model and separate it from additive light mixing, tying colour order to the physical wave property that dispersion sorts.
learnerActions: Order the visible spectrum by increasing frequency (red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength → violet = highest frequency/shortest).
Predict and explain the colour of a red object seen under blue light, and of a white and a black object under the same light.
Match an object plus an illuminating colour to the perceived colour.

Predict what is seen when white light passes through a red filter, and explain why an opaque coloured object behaves like a selective filter, except that it selects the light it reflects rather than the light it transmits.
Predict the result of overlapping red and green spotlights and explain why it is yellow, not brown.
Explain why a prism disperses white light and why a second prism can recombine the spectrum to white.
activities.title: Reason about colour: spectrum order, filters, and prisms
